**Voltage tells us how much electrical energy can be transferred for a certain amount of electric charge between two places.**

That is a lot of new words in one sentence. To understand it, we need to understand **charge**, **energy**, and what it means for something to move between two places.

We can start with atoms.

Things such as your body, your clothes, a battery, and a metal wire are made of **atoms**. Atoms are so small that you cannot see one just by looking carefully with your eyes.

Atoms have smaller parts:

- **Protons** have positive electric charge.
- **Electrons** have negative electric charge.
- **Neutrons** have no overall electric charge.

Protons and neutrons are together in the middle of an atom. That middle part is called the **nucleus**. Electrons occupy the space around the nucleus. They do not follow little circular paths in the way they are sometimes drawn in pictures.

**Electric charge is a property of a particle.** It helps determine how the particle affects other charged particles.

Here are the basic rules:

- Two positive charges repel each other.
- Two negative charges repel each other.
- A positive charge and a negative charge attract each other.

“Repel” means that they exert forces that tend to move them apart. “Attract” means that they exert forces that tend to move them toward each other.

Those are real physical forces.

Every electron has the same amount of negative charge. Every proton has an equal amount of positive charge.

An atom with the same number of electrons and protons has no overall charge. We call it **electrically neutral**. The positive and negative charges add up to zero.

The charged parts are still there. Being neutral does not mean having no charged particles.

An atom can sometimes gain or lose electrons. If it gains extra electrons, it becomes negatively charged. If it loses electrons, it becomes positively charged. A charged atom is called an **ion**.

Now we can talk about electricity.

**Electricity is the name we give to many things that happen because of electric charges.** Charges can exert forces, collect on objects, move through materials, and transfer energy.

Electricity does not always mean that electrons are moving through a wire. For example, an object can have extra electric charge even when that charge is mostly staying in place. That is part of what we call **static electricity**.

But moving charges are very important in electrical devices.

In a metal wire, some electrons can move through the metal. They are not permanently attached to just one atom. The nuclei of the metal atoms mostly remain in their usual positions, though they vibrate.

When there is an overall movement of charge, we call that an **electric current**.

So:

**Current tells us how much charge passes a place each second.**

More charge passing each second means more current.

Even when a metal wire has no current, its electrons are not all perfectly still. They move around. But without an overall movement of charge in a particular direction, there is no net current through the wire.

To understand voltage, we also need energy.

**Energy is something we keep track of when things move, heat up, give off light, or change in other ways.**

A moving object has energy because of its motion. A hot object has energy associated with the motion and interactions of its tiny parts. A battery can provide energy through chemical changes inside it.

Energy can move from one thing to another. It can also change form.

For example, when a battery powers a lamp, some of the energy from the battery becomes light, and some becomes heat.

The energy does not simply disappear.

Electric charges can have **electrical potential energy** because of their positions and their interactions with other charges. Moving a charge to a different place can change that energy.

That brings us back to voltage.

**Voltage measures the difference in electrical potential energy per amount of charge between two places.**

The words **“per amount of charge”** matter.

Voltage does not tell us the total energy transferred by an entire battery. It tells us how much energy can be transferred for each unit of charge.

We measure voltage in **volts**, written **V**.

A small battery might have a voltage of **1.5 V** between its two ends. Another battery might have **9 V**.

For the same amount of charge moving through a complete external circuit, a 9 V battery can provide six times as much electrical energy as a 1.5 V battery.

That does **not** mean the 9 V battery necessarily lasts six times as long. How long a battery lasts also depends on how much energy it stores and how quickly the connected device uses that energy.

Here is the important measurement rule:

**One volt means one joule of energy per coulomb of charge.**

A **joule**, written **J**, is a unit of energy.

A **coulomb**, written **C**, is a unit of electric charge.

One electron carries a very tiny amount of charge. It takes about **6,240,000,000,000,000,000 electrons** to make up a total negative charge with a size of one coulomb.

You do not need to memorize that number. It just tells us that a coulomb includes the charge of very many electrons.

For a 1.5 V battery:

**1.5 volts = 1.5 joules per coulomb.**

If one coulomb of charge passes through a lamp connected across that battery, about 1.5 joules of electrical energy can be transferred to the lamp, assuming the battery keeps that voltage and the wires lose very little energy.

If two coulombs pass through, that is about 3 joules.

The voltage stayed the same. More energy was transferred because more charge passed through.

This is why we need to keep **charge** and **energy** separate in our thinking.

An electron has electric charge. It can gain or lose energy while keeping exactly the same charge.

A lamp does not use up the electrons that pass through it. It receives energy.

Now, why does a battery have voltage?

A battery contains materials that can undergo chemical reactions. Those reactions can move charges and maintain an electrical difference between the battery’s two terminals.

The **terminals** are the places where you connect wires. They are marked **positive, +**, and **negative, −**.

When you connect a suitable circuit, chemical changes inside the battery provide energy while charge moves around the circuit.

A **circuit** is an arrangement of connected electrical parts. For a battery to keep supplying a steady current through a lamp, there must be a complete conducting path from one battery terminal, through the lamp, to the other terminal. Charge also moves inside the battery as part of its chemical processes.

Inside the metal wires, electrons carry the current. Inside the battery, moving ions also help complete the process.

The battery does not need to create all the electrons in the wires. The wires already contain electrons.

When the circuit is connected, the arrangement of charges produces an **electric field** in and around the circuit.

An electric field describes the electric force that a charge would experience at a place.

Electrons in the wire respond to that field. This produces their overall movement through the circuit.

An individual electron usually moves along the wire quite slowly on average. But the electrical change that causes electrons throughout the circuit to respond spreads very quickly.

That is why a lamp can turn on quickly without waiting for one particular electron to travel all the way from the battery to the lamp.

There is another important point:

**Voltage can exist even when there is no steady current.**

An unconnected battery still has voltage between its terminals.

But with no complete conducting path, it cannot keep sending a current through an external device.

An ordinary switch uses this fact.

When the switch is open, it interrupts the conducting path. There may still be voltage between parts of the circuit, but there is no continuing current through that broken path.

When the switch closes, it completes the path, and current can flow.

So voltage and current are different things:

- **Voltage:** how much energy can be transferred per unit of charge between two places.
- **Current:** how much charge passes a place each second.

Current is measured in **amperes**, usually called **amps**, written **A**.

**One amp means one coulomb of charge passes a place each second.**

A circuit carrying two amps has twice as much charge passing each second as a circuit carrying one amp.

But knowing the voltage alone does not tell us the current.

We also need to know what is connected.

That brings us to **resistance**.

Resistance describes how much a part opposes electric current.

In many materials, moving electrons interact with the material and transfer energy to it. This can make the material warmer.

A part called a **resistor** is made to provide a chosen amount of resistance.

Resistance is measured in **ohms**, written with the symbol **Ω**.

For a resistor whose resistance stays the same, the relationship is:

**Current = voltage ÷ resistance**

This is **Ohm’s law**.

It is often written:

**I = V ÷ R**

Here:

- **I** means current in amps.
- **V** means voltage in volts.
- **R** means resistance in ohms.

The letter **I** is just the letter scientists use for current in this equation.

Suppose a 6 V battery is connected across a 3 Ω resistor.

Then:

**6 ÷ 3 = 2**

The current is **2 A**.

Now suppose we use the same 6 V battery with a 6 Ω resistor.

Then:

**6 ÷ 6 = 1**

The current is **1 A**.

With the same voltage, the larger resistance gives a smaller current.

Or suppose we keep the 3 Ω resistor and reduce the voltage to 3 V.

Then:

**3 ÷ 3 = 1**

The current is again **1 A**.

For that same resistor, a smaller voltage gives a smaller current.

Ohm’s law works especially simply for parts whose resistance stays fairly constant. Some electrical parts behave differently. For example, an LED does not have one fixed resistance that describes everything it does.

There is also a useful way to connect voltage and current to energy.

**Power tells us how quickly energy is being transferred.**

Power is measured in **watts**, written **W**.

One watt means one joule of energy transferred each second.

For a simple battery circuit:

**Power = voltage × current**

Suppose a device has 6 V across it and a current of 2 A through it.

Then:

**6 × 2 = 12**

The device receives electrical energy at a rate of **12 W**.

That means **12 joules each second**.

You can see why both voltage and current matter:

The voltage tells us the energy transferred per coulomb.

The current tells us the coulombs passing each second.

Multiplying them tells us the energy transferred each second.

Now there is one part of voltage that can seem strange at first:

**Voltage is a difference between two places.**

To measure it, a voltmeter has two connections. Each connection touches a different place in the circuit. The meter compares those places.

When someone says, “This point is at 5 volts,” they mean it is 5 volts compared with some chosen reference point.

That reference point is often called **ground** and is assigned a value of **0 V**.

In a small battery circuit, ground might simply be the battery’s negative terminal. It does not have to be connected to the soil.

Calling something 0 V does not mean it contains no electrons, no electric charge, or no energy. It tells us which reference we are using.

The difference between 5 V and 0 V is 5 V.

The difference between 105 V and 100 V is also 5 V.

For electrical effects between those two points, that difference matters.

A related detail concerns the direction of current.

In ordinary metal wires connected to a battery, electrons move overall from the negative terminal, through the external circuit, toward the positive terminal.

But the direction called **conventional current** is the opposite: from positive to negative through the external circuit.

That naming rule was established before scientists understood electrons.

Both descriptions can be used correctly, as long as we know which one we mean.

The negative charge of an electron also means something important: **an electron moving toward a higher voltage can lose electrical potential energy**.

So it would be incorrect to say that every kind of charge must lose energy by moving toward a lower voltage. Positive and negative charges behave differently.

You do not need that detail to use a simple battery circuit, but it helps keep the explanation accurate.

Finally, a battery and a wall outlet provide different kinds of voltage.

A battery usually maintains the same polarity: the terminal marked positive stays positive compared with the terminal marked negative. In a simple resistor circuit, this produces **direct current**, or **DC**, which keeps the same direction.

A wall outlet provides **alternating voltage**. Its polarity reverses repeatedly. In many connected devices, that causes the current to reverse repeatedly too. This is **alternating current**, or **AC**.

Electrical energy can still be transferred even though the electrons repeatedly change their direction of motion.

The central ideas are these:

**Charge** is a property of particles such as electrons and protons.

**Current** is the rate at which charge passes a place.

**Voltage** is the electrical energy difference per unit of charge between two places.

**Resistance** helps determine how much current a given voltage produces.

**Power** is the rate at which energy is transferred.

When a battery lights a lamp, charge moves around the completed circuit, and energy is transferred from the battery to the lamp. The lamp gives off light and heat. The electrons keep their charge.

**Voltage tells us how much energy can be transferred for each amount of charge that moves between the two places being compared.**

answer:
**Voltage tells us how much electrical energy can be transferred for a certain amount of electric charge moving between two places.**

That is a lot of new words. We can understand it by learning what each part means: **electric charge**, **energy**, and **two places**.

Let’s start with what things are made of.

Almost everything you touch is made of **atoms**. Your hands, your clothes, the ground, and the metal inside a wire are made of atoms.

Atoms are extremely small. You cannot see one with your eyes.

An atom has different parts:

- **Protons**, which have positive electric charge.
- **Electrons**, which have negative electric charge.
- Usually, **neutrons**, which have no electric charge.

The protons and neutrons are together in the middle of the atom. This middle part is called the **nucleus**. Electrons occupy the space around the nucleus.

Electrons are not alive. They do not choose where to go. Their motion follows the laws of physics.

**Electric charge is a property of matter.**

A property is something we can describe or measure about a thing. Mass is a property. Electric charge is another property.

There are two kinds of electric charge: positive and negative.

The names “positive” and “negative” do not mean good and bad. They simply name the two kinds.

Electric charges exert forces on one another:

- Two positive charges repel each other.
- Two negative charges repel each other.
- A positive charge and a negative charge attract each other.

“Attract” means the force acts to bring them closer together. “Repel” means the force acts to move them farther apart.

These forces can exist even when the charged objects are not touching.

An electron has a certain amount of negative charge. A proton has an equal amount of positive charge.

When an atom has the same number of electrons and protons, those charges add up to zero. We call the atom **electrically neutral**.

Neutral does not mean there are no charges inside. It means the positive and negative amounts balance.

An atom can gain an electron or lose an electron. Then its total charge is no longer zero. An atom with a total electric charge is called an **ion**.

An object can also gain or lose electrons. If it gains extra electrons, it becomes negatively charged. If it loses electrons, it becomes positively charged.

Usually, when ordinary objects become charged, electrons move from one object to another. Protons stay inside their atoms’ nuclei.

Now we can talk about **electricity**.

“Electricity” is a broad word. It includes things that happen because electric charges exist, exert forces, or move.

Electricity includes the charge that can collect on an object. It also includes the electric current in a working lamp.

Those are related, but they are not exactly the same thing.

To understand voltage, we also need to understand **energy**.

Energy is something physical systems can transfer. Transferring energy can cause changes.

For example:

- A lamp receives energy and produces light and heat.
- A motor receives energy and makes something move.
- A heater receives energy and warms up.

Energy does not simply disappear when a device uses it. It changes form or moves somewhere else.

A lamp does not destroy energy. It transfers energy into light and heat.

We measure energy in units called **joules**.

You do not need to know exactly how big a joule is yet. For now, remember:

**Joules measure amounts of energy.**

We also have a unit for electric charge. It is called the **coulomb**.

One electron has a very small amount of charge. A coulomb is a much larger amount. It takes about 6.24 billion billion electrons to have a total charge of negative one coulomb.

That is an enormous number because each electron’s charge is so small.

Now we have two measurements:

- **Joules** tell us how much energy.
- **Coulombs** tell us how much electric charge.

**Voltage connects those two measurements.**

One volt means **one joule of energy per coulomb of charge**.

Written with symbols:

**1 volt = 1 joule ÷ 1 coulomb**

The word **per** is important. Voltage does not tell us the total amount of energy by itself. It tells us the amount of energy for each amount of charge.

Suppose a battery has a voltage of 3 volts.

In an ideal circuit, that battery can supply about 3 joules of electrical energy for each coulomb of charge that passes through it.

If 2 coulombs pass through, it supplies about 6 joules.

If 3 coulombs pass through, it supplies about 9 joules.

The voltage stays at 3 volts in this example. The total energy increases because more charge passes through.

So:

**Voltage tells us energy per charge, rather than total energy.**

There is another important part: **voltage is a difference between two places**.

A battery has two metal connections called **terminals**. One is marked plus, and the other is marked minus.

If a battery is labeled 1.5 volts, that means the voltage difference between its terminals is about 1.5 volts.

The plus terminal is at a higher **electric potential** than the minus terminal.

“Electric potential” is the name for the energy-per-charge value at a place, compared with a chosen reference. The difference between the values at two places is voltage.

That is why another name for voltage is **electric potential difference**.

You do not need to memorize that name. The important part is that there are **two places being compared**.

When someone says, “This wire is at 5 volts,” they mean it is at 5 volts compared with some other place in the circuit. Often, that other place has been chosen as zero volts.

Choosing zero does not mean that place has no electrons or no electric activity. It gives us a reference for our measurements.

You can measure a voltage between two places using an instrument called a **voltmeter**. It has two measuring connections because it compares two places.

But what does a voltage have to do with things moving?

Charged particles respond to an **electric field**.

An electric field is a physical condition in a region that can exert a force on electric charge. You cannot see the field directly, but you can measure its effects.

A battery connected to a circuit helps establish an electric field in the circuit. That field exerts forces on the movable charges.

Positive and negative charges respond in opposite directions.

A positive charge experiences a force in the direction of the electric field. An electron, because it is negative, experiences a force in the opposite direction.

That difference matters. We cannot say that every kind of charge moves toward the same battery terminal.

In an ordinary metal circuit powered by a battery, the electrons’ average motion through the external circuit is from the negative terminal toward the positive terminal.

As they move through a device such as a resistor, energy is transferred to the material. The material can become warmer.

The moving electrons are still electrons afterward. Their charge has not been used up.

**A device receives energy. It does not use up electric charge.**

Now we can distinguish voltage from **electric current**.

Electric current tells us how much electric charge passes a place each second.

We measure current in **amperes**, usually shortened to **amps**.

**1 amp means 1 coulomb of charge passes each second.**

Compare the two ideas:

- **Voltage:** how much energy can be transferred per coulomb.
- **Current:** how many coulombs pass each second.

Those are different measurements.

A battery can have voltage even when it is sitting on a table with nothing connected to it. Its two terminals still have a voltage difference.

But there is almost no continuing current through the surrounding air because air normally does not allow charges to move through it easily.

So **voltage can exist without a continuing current**.

To get a steady current from a battery through a device, we usually connect a complete circuit.

For example, we can connect:

1. One battery terminal to a lamp.
2. The other side of the lamp to the other battery terminal.

The battery, wires, and lamp then form a complete conducting connection.

If we break that connection with an open switch, the continuing current stops. The battery can still have voltage between its terminals.

Inside a metal wire, some electrons can move throughout the metal. They are already there before the battery is connected.

The battery does not have to fill an empty wire with electrons.

When the circuit is connected, the electric field changes throughout the circuit. Electrons in different parts of the wire respond.

The electrons already have complicated motion. The current involves a small average movement added to that motion. This average movement is often quite slow.

The electrical effect can spread through the circuit much faster than individual electrons travel around it. That is why a lamp can turn on quickly.

Where does the battery get the energy?

**A battery stores energy in its chemical substances.**

Chemical reactions inside the battery transfer energy and help maintain the voltage between its terminals.

When the battery supplies a working circuit, stored chemical energy decreases. Electrical energy is transferred to the circuit, and some energy also becomes heat inside the battery.

A battery eventually stops working well because the chemical changes it can use become limited.

It has not simply “run out of electrons.” There are still enormous numbers of electrons in it.

Next comes **resistance**.

Resistance tells us how much a part of a circuit opposes electric current for a given voltage.

Some materials allow charge to move easily. We call them **conductors**. Copper is a good conductor, which is why it is often used in wires.

Other materials allow very little charge movement under ordinary conditions. We call them **insulators**. Many plastics are good insulators.

Resistance depends on several things, including:

- What the material is.
- How long it is.
- How thick it is.
- Its temperature.

For wires made of the same material at the same temperature, a longer wire usually has more resistance. A thicker wire usually has less resistance.

We measure resistance in **ohms**. The symbol for an ohm is **Ω**.

For many materials and components under suitable conditions, voltage, current, and resistance are related by **Ohm’s law**:

**Voltage = current × resistance**

In symbols:

**V = I × R**

Here:

- **V** means voltage, measured in volts.
- **I** means current, measured in amps.
- **R** means resistance, measured in ohms.

We can also write it this way:

**Current = voltage ÷ resistance**

Imagine an ideal resistor with a resistance of 3 ohms.

If the voltage across it is 6 volts:

**6 volts ÷ 3 ohms = 2 amps**

So the current through it is 2 amps.

If we keep the resistance at 3 ohms but increase the voltage to 12 volts:

**12 volts ÷ 3 ohms = 4 amps**

The voltage doubled, and the current doubled.

Now keep the voltage at 6 volts, but use a resistance of 6 ohms:

**6 volts ÷ 6 ohms = 1 amp**

The resistance doubled, and the current became half as much.

For a fixed resistance:

**More voltage produces more current.**

For a fixed voltage:

**More resistance produces less current.**

These rules work when the component’s resistance stays constant. Some devices, including LEDs, do not have a simple constant resistance. Even a lamp’s filament changes resistance as it gets hotter. We cannot treat every device as one fixed resistor.

There is one more useful idea: **power**.

Power tells us how quickly energy is transferred.

We measure power in **watts**.

**1 watt means 1 joule of energy transferred each second.**

For a simple battery-powered device:

**Power = voltage × current**

For example, if a device has 3 volts across it and a current of 2 amps through it:

**3 volts × 2 amps = 6 watts**

That means the device receives 6 joules of electrical energy each second.

This makes sense from what the units mean:

- Each coulomb transfers 3 joules.
- Two coulombs pass each second.
- Therefore, 6 joules are transferred each second.

Voltage alone does not tell us the power. We need to know the current too.

And voltage alone does not tell us how long a battery will last. Two batteries can have the same voltage while storing different amounts of energy.

One final detail helps explain why electricity can do different things.

In an ordinary resistor, electrical energy mainly becomes heat as moving charges interact with the material.

In an LED, some electrical energy becomes light.

In a motor, electrical forces and magnetic forces help produce motion.

The charges do not decide what to make. The materials and arrangement of the device determine what happens.

So when you see a voltage written on a battery, remember what that number describes:

**It tells you how much electrical energy the battery can supply for each amount of charge passing through it.**

A 1.5-volt battery can supply about **1.5 joules per coulomb**. A 9-volt battery can supply about **9 joules per coulomb**.

That energy can become light, heat, sound, or motion when there is a suitable circuit.

**Voltage is the difference in electrical energy per charge between two places. Current is how quickly charge moves past a place. They describe different parts of what electricity is doing.**

answer:
**Voltage tells us how much electrical energy can be transferred for a certain amount of electric charge moving between two places.**

We measure voltage in **volts**, written **V**. When a battery says “1.5 V,” that describes the voltage between its two ends.

To understand what that means, we need to understand electric charge, energy, and movement.

Your body, a metal wire, and a battery all contain **atoms**. Atoms are extremely small pieces of matter.

An atom contains several kinds of particles:

- **Protons**, which have positive electric charge.
- **Electrons**, which have negative electric charge.
- **Neutrons**, which have no electric charge.

Protons are in the atom’s central part, called its **nucleus**. Most atoms also have neutrons there. Electrons are found around the nucleus.

**Electric charge is a property of these particles.** It affects how they exert electric forces on one another.

Two positive charges repel each other. That means each experiences a force away from the other.

Two negative charges also repel each other.

A positive charge and a negative charge attract each other. Each experiences a force toward the other.

Every electron has the same amount of negative charge. Every proton has an equal amount of positive charge.

An atom with equal numbers of protons and electrons has zero total charge. We call it **electrically neutral**. Its positive and negative charges add up to zero.

An atom can gain or lose electrons. When that happens, it has a total charge and is called an **ion**.

An atom that gains an electron becomes negatively charged. An atom that loses an electron becomes positively charged.

These facts help explain both electricity in wires and electricity inside batteries.

**Electricity is a name for physical effects involving electric charge.**

Sometimes electric charge builds up on something. Sometimes charge moves through a material. Sometimes changing electric and magnetic fields transfer energy.

All of those involve electricity.

A metal wire already contains electrons before we connect it to a battery.

In a metal, some electrons can move throughout the material. The atoms mostly remain in their positions, although they vibrate.

Materials that let electric charge move easily are called **conductors**. Copper and aluminum are conductors, which is why they are often used in wires.

Materials in which electric charge moves much less easily are called **insulators**. Plastic and glass are examples.

The plastic covering on a wire helps keep electric charge from moving between the metal wire and things touching the covering.

Now we need another idea: **energy**.

Energy can be transferred and can change form. It is involved when something moves, heats up, or gives off light.

A battery has energy available from chemical reactions.

A lamp receives electrical energy and transfers it into light and heat.

A motor receives electrical energy and transfers some of it into movement. Some also becomes heat.

We measure energy in a unit called the **joule**, written **J**.

Electric charge has its own unit: the **coulomb**, written **C**.

One electron has an extremely small amount of charge. It takes an enormous number of electrons to make one coulomb of negative charge.

So we have two different things to measure:

- **Joules** measure energy.
- **Coulombs** measure electric charge.

That lets us explain voltage precisely.

**One volt means one joule of energy for each coulomb of charge.**

Written with unit names:

**1 volt = 1 joule per coulomb**

“Per” means “for each.”

A voltage difference tells us how much the electrical energy changes for each coulomb moving between the two places. Depending on the charge and which way it moves, it can gain or lose electrical energy.

For a device receiving electrical energy, we can write:

**Energy received = voltage across the device × charge passing through it**

Suppose a lamp has **3 volts** across its connections.

If **1 coulomb** of charge passes through it, the lamp receives:

**3 × 1 = 3 joules**

If **2 coulombs** pass through it, the lamp receives:

**3 × 2 = 6 joules**

The voltage stayed the same. More charge passed through, so more energy was transferred.

Now suppose a lamp has **6 volts** across it.

Each coulomb passing through transfers **6 joules**.

That is what a higher voltage means: **more energy transferred for the same amount of charge.**

It does not tell us, by itself, how much charge actually moves.

**Voltage is always between two places.**

For a battery, we usually mean the voltage between its two terminals. A terminal is a connection point.

One terminal is marked **+**. The other is marked **−**.

A 1.5-volt battery has a difference of 1.5 volts between those terminals.

The more technical name for voltage is **electric potential difference**.

When someone says, “This point is at 5 volts,” they mean it is 5 volts compared with some other point they have chosen as a reference.

That reference is often called **ground** in an electrical circuit. Ground is assigned a value of zero volts.

Zero volts at that reference does not mean there are zero electrons there. It means we are measuring voltage differences starting from that chosen value.

A voltage measurement needs two connections because it compares two places.

That is why a **voltmeter**, the instrument used to measure voltage, has two leads. One connects to each place being compared.

**A battery maintains a voltage using chemical reactions.**

Those reactions act on charged particles inside the battery. They supply energy that maintains the difference between its terminals.

When the battery powers a device, chemical energy becomes electrical energy, which the device receives.

The battery already contains charged particles. So do the wires and the device. The battery does not need to create new electrons.

Inside the battery, moving ions and chemical reactions are part of how the current continues. In the metal wires outside the battery, electrons move.

A battery can have a voltage even when it is disconnected from everything.

This is an important fact:

**Voltage can exist without a continuing electric current.**

An unused battery can still have 1.5 volts between its terminals. Its voltage is there even though it is not powering a lamp.

To understand what happens when we connect the lamp, we need to distinguish voltage from **current**.

**Electric current measures how much charge passes a place each second.**

We measure current in **amperes**, usually shortened to **amps**, written **A**.

One amp means:

**1 coulomb of charge passing each second**

Two amps means:

**2 coulombs of charge passing each second**

So voltage and current answer different questions:

- **Voltage:** How much energy can be transferred for each coulomb?
- **Current:** How many coulombs pass each second?

A circuit can have a voltage between two points while having no steady current through a device.

Now imagine an actual circuit containing a battery, two wires, a switch, and a lamp.

The connections make a complete path from one battery terminal, through the lamp, to the other terminal. The battery’s internal processes complete the circuit.

When the switch is closed, a steady current can flow.

When the switch is open, the path is interrupted. The steady current through the lamp stops.

The battery can still have a voltage between its terminals while the switch is open.

**Electric fields exert the forces that affect the charges.**

An electric field is a physical condition in space that can exert an electric force on a charged particle.

Electric charges produce electric fields.

When a battery is connected into a circuit, the charges in and around the circuit adjust. An electric field develops along the conducting path.

That field exerts forces on the electrons in the wires.

The electrons already have motion within the metal. With current, their motion also has an overall direction. This overall movement is called **drift**.

In an ordinary metal circuit powered by a battery, electrons drift through the external circuit from the negative terminal toward the positive terminal.

Scientists define the direction of current as the direction a positive charge would move. This is called **conventional current**.

So, in that same external circuit:

- Electron drift is from **− toward +**.
- Conventional current is from **+ toward −**.

Both descriptions concern the same circuit. The difference comes from electrons having negative charge.

Voltage and electric force are connected, but they measure different things.

Voltage concerns the change in electrical energy per charge between two places.

Electric force concerns how a charged particle is being pushed or pulled at a particular place. That force depends on the electric field there.

**The electrons do not need to travel all the way from the battery before the lamp starts responding.**

There are already electrons throughout the wires and lamp.

When the circuit is completed, changes in the electric and magnetic fields spread through the circuit very quickly. Those fields transfer energy from the battery to the lamp.

The electrons’ average drift through a metal wire can be quite slow. The electrical effect spreads much faster.

That explains why a lamp can respond quickly even though individual electrons drift slowly.

We can now add **resistance**.

**Resistance describes how much a material or component limits current for a given voltage.**

We measure resistance in **ohms**, written with this symbol: **Ω**.

A component made to provide a particular resistance is called a **resistor**.

For many ordinary resistors:

- Increasing the voltage increases the current.
- Increasing the resistance decreases the current for the same voltage.

In a metal, electrons interact with the material as they move. Electrical energy can be transferred into the material, making it warmer.

That is why a resistor carrying current often heats up.

A wire also has resistance, although a suitable connecting wire usually has very little.

Resistance depends on several things, including:

- What the material is.
- How long the conductor is.
- How thick it is.
- Its temperature.

For wires made from the same material at the same temperature, a longer wire has more resistance. A thicker wire has less resistance.

The relationship between voltage, current, and resistance is called **Ohm’s law**.

It is commonly written:

**V = I × R**

The letters mean:

- **V** is voltage, measured in volts.
- **I** is current, measured in amps.
- **R** is resistance, measured in ohms.

We can also write it this way:

**Current = voltage ÷ resistance**

Let’s use small numbers.

Suppose a resistor has a resistance of **3 ohms**, and there are **3 volts** across it.

The current is:

**3 ÷ 3 = 1 amp**

Now increase the voltage to **6 volts**, keeping the resistance at **3 ohms**.

The current becomes:

**6 ÷ 3 = 2 amps**

Twice the voltage produces twice the current because the resistance stayed the same.

Instead, suppose we keep the voltage at **3 volts** and use a resistance of **6 ohms**.

The current is:

**3 ÷ 6 = 0.5 amp**

That is half an amp.

| Voltage | Resistance | Current |
|---|---|---|
| 3 volts | 3 ohms | 1 amp |
| 6 volts | 3 ohms | 2 amps |
| 3 volts | 6 ohms | Half an amp |

Ohm’s law works especially well for components whose resistance stays approximately constant.

Real components can become warmer, and their resistance can change. Some components, such as LEDs, have a more complicated relationship between voltage and current.

So doubling the voltage does not always double the current in every possible device.

**Current is not used up as it passes through a resistor or lamp.**

In a steady circuit with one path, charge enters and leaves the component at the same rate.

If one coulomb enters each second, one coulomb leaves each second.

The component receives **energy**. It does not continually collect all the charge passing through it.

This distinction explains how the same current can pass through several components while each receives some energy.

Suppose a battery provides **3 volts**, and two resistors are connected one after the other. This is called a **series connection**.

The same steady current passes through both resistors.

The voltage across the first resistor and the voltage across the second add up to the battery’s 3 volts, assuming the connecting wires have negligible resistance.

If the resistors are identical, each has 1.5 volts across it.

Each receives part of the energy supplied for every coulomb that passes through the circuit.

There is another way to connect components: **in parallel**.

In a parallel connection, each component connects between the same two points.

If two lamps are each connected directly across a 3-volt battery, each has 3 volts across it.

Current divides between the two paths. The battery supplies the total current needed by both.

These arrangements show why it matters to say exactly **where** we are measuring voltage.

Voltage across the battery, voltage across one component, and voltage across another component can have different values.

**Voltage and current together tell us how quickly electrical energy is transferred.**

The rate of energy transfer is called **power**.

We measure power in **watts**, written **W**.

One watt means:

**1 joule transferred each second**

For a simple direct-current circuit:

**Power = voltage × current**

Or, using letters:

**P = V × I**

Suppose a device has **3 volts** across it and **1 amp** through it.

Its electrical power is:

**3 × 1 = 3 watts**

We can understand that from the units:

The voltage says each coulomb transfers **3 joules**.

The current says **1 coulomb passes each second**.

Therefore, **3 joules transfer each second**.

That is 3 watts.

If the same device operated at that power for 10 seconds, it would receive:

**3 joules each second × 10 seconds = 30 joules**

These quantities describe different parts of what is happening:

- **Volts:** energy transferred per amount of charge.
- **Amps:** charge passing per second.
- **Ohms:** resistance to current for a given voltage.
- **Watts:** energy transferred per second.
- **Joules:** an amount of energy.

This also explains why a battery’s voltage does not tell us how long it will last.

Two batteries can have the same voltage but store different amounts of usable energy.

A battery maintaining 1.5 volts supplies about 1.5 joules for each coulomb passing through the external circuit. How much total energy it can supply also depends on how much charge its chemical reactions can move before it is depleted.

How long it lasts depends on how quickly the connected device takes energy.

As a battery becomes depleted, its chemical condition changes. It may no longer maintain enough voltage while supplying the current the device needs.

**Battery voltage also depends on how batteries are connected.**

Two 1.5-volt batteries connected in series, with the positive terminal of one connected to the negative terminal of the other, provide about **3 volts** between the two remaining terminals.

Their voltage differences add:

**1.5 + 1.5 = 3 volts**

That is why a device may use several batteries.

The device’s parts need a suitable voltage to operate as intended. Applying a different voltage changes the electrical conditions inside it.

Finally, voltage can stay in one direction or change direction repeatedly.

An ordinary battery is a **direct-current source**, usually called **DC**. While it is supplying power normally, its positive terminal remains positive compared with its negative terminal.

Its exact voltage can change as it is used.

Household electrical supplies usually provide **alternating voltage**, associated with **alternating current**, or **AC**.

With alternating voltage, which connection has the higher electric potential changes repeatedly.

In metal wires carrying AC, the electrons’ overall drift reverses repeatedly. Electrical energy can still be transferred to an appliance while that happens.

For one complete numerical example, consider a **3-volt battery** connected through a closed switch to a **3-ohm resistor**, using wires with very little resistance.

Ohm’s law gives:

**Current = 3 volts ÷ 3 ohms = 1 amp**

That means one coulomb passes through the resistor each second.

The 3-volt difference means each coulomb transfers 3 joules to the resistor.

So the resistor receives:

**3 joules each second = 3 watts**

That energy becomes heat.

After 5 seconds, the resistor has received:

**3 × 5 = 15 joules**

Open the switch, and the steady current stops. The resistor stops receiving that continuing supply of electrical energy.

The battery can still have **3 volts between its terminals**. Its voltage describes the energy available per charge, even while no steady current flows.

answer:
**Voltage tells us how much energy can be transferred when a certain amount of electric charge moves between two places.**

We measure voltage in **volts**. The letter **V** stands for volts. A battery marked “1.5 V” has a voltage of 1.5 volts between its two connection points.

To understand what that means, we need to understand charge, energy, and movement. Let’s start with the tiny things inside ordinary objects.

Your body, air, water, and metal wires contain **atoms**. Atoms are extremely small. You cannot see individual atoms with your eyes.

Atoms contain smaller particles:

- **Protons** have positive electric charge.
- **Electrons** have negative electric charge.
- **Neutrons** have no electric charge.

Protons are in the atom’s central part, called the **nucleus**. Most nuclei also contain neutrons. Electrons are found in regions around the nucleus.

**Electric charge** is a property of these particles. It determines how they take part in electrical forces.

Two positively charged particles repel each other: each experiences a force away from the other.

Two negatively charged particles also repel each other.

A positively charged particle and a negatively charged particle attract each other: each experiences a force toward the other.

The words “positive” and “negative” name the two kinds of charge.

An electron’s negative charge and a proton’s positive charge have exactly the same size. Their signs are opposite.

If an atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, its total charge is zero. We call it **electrically neutral**.

If that atom gains an extra electron, it becomes negatively charged. If it loses an electron, it becomes positively charged. An atom with an overall electric charge is called an **ion**.

An electrically neutral object still contains electric charges. It has equal amounts of positive and negative charge overall.

In a metal wire, some electrons can move through the metal. The atoms’ nuclei stay near their positions in the solid, while these electrons can move throughout it.

That movement matters because **moving electric charge is an electric current**.

In metal wires, electrons carry the current. In other materials, other charged particles can carry current. For example, positive and negative ions can move through salty water.

Electricity includes electric charges, the forces between them, and what happens when they move or rearrange.

Now we need another important word: **energy**.

Energy is a quantity that helps us describe physical changes and how much change can happen.

A lamp receives energy and gives off light and heat.

An electric motor receives energy and makes parts move.

An electric heater receives energy and warms up.

A battery stores energy in its chemicals. Chemical reactions allow the battery to transfer some of that energy to a circuit.

We measure energy in **joules**, written **J**.

Charge and energy are different quantities. An electron has a particular amount of electric charge, but the amount of energy it has can change.

One kind of energy is **electric potential energy**. This energy depends on how charges are arranged and where they are relative to one another.

For example, separating two particles that attract each other requires energy. When they move closer together because of their attraction, electric potential energy can become energy of motion.

So the position of a charge matters. The same particle can have different electric potential energy in different places.

This brings us back to voltage.

**Voltage compares two places. It tells us the difference in electric potential energy for each amount of charge.**

The words **“for each”** are especially important.

We need a way to measure an amount of charge. The unit we use is the **coulomb**, written **C**.

One electron has a very small amount of charge. About six billion billion electrons together have a negative charge whose size is one coulomb.

You do not need to remember that enormous number. The important idea is that a coulomb is a measured amount of charge.

Now we can say exactly what a volt means:

**One volt means one joule for each coulomb.**

Written with units:

**1 V = 1 J/C**

The slash means “for each,” or “per.”

So:

- **1 volt** means **1 joule per coulomb**.
- **3 volts** means **3 joules per coulomb**.
- **9 volts** means **9 joules per coulomb**.

Suppose a lamp has a voltage of 3 volts between its two connections.

As one coulomb of charge passes through the lamp, 3 joules of electrical energy are transferred to the lamp. The lamp produces light and heat.

If two coulombs pass through at that same voltage, 6 joules are transferred.

If three coulombs pass through, 9 joules are transferred.

The relationship is:

**Energy transferred = voltage × amount of charge**

More charge passing through can transfer more energy. A larger voltage can also mean more energy transferred for the same amount of charge.

Voltage alone does not tell us how quickly that happens. We will need current for that.

First, notice that voltage is always a comparison **between two places**.

A battery has two connection points, called **terminals**. One is marked **+**, and the other is marked **−**.

When we say a battery is 1.5 volts, we mean there is a 1.5-volt difference between those terminals.

When someone says, “This point in a circuit is at 5 volts,” they mean it is 5 volts higher than some chosen reference point.

That reference point is often called **ground** and is assigned a voltage of zero. In a circuit, “ground” can simply mean the point chosen for comparison; it does not always mean a connection to the soil.

There is a detail about positive and negative charge that helps explain what electrons do.

A **positive charge** has more electric potential energy at a higher voltage.

An **electron**, because its charge is negative, has less electric potential energy at a higher voltage.

In an ordinary battery circuit, electrons move through the outside wires from the battery’s negative terminal toward its positive terminal. As they pass through components such as a lamp, electrical energy can be transferred to those components.

The signs matter because positive and negative charges respond to electrical forces in opposite directions.

How does a battery keep its terminals at different voltages?

**Chemical reactions inside the battery move charges and maintain the voltage difference.**

Those reactions use the battery’s stored chemical energy.

A battery does not need to create new electrons. The materials in the battery and the wires already contain electrons.

As the battery operates, its chemicals change. Eventually, its chemical state can no longer maintain enough voltage while supplying the needed current. The device then stops working properly.

That is what happens when a battery runs down.

Imagine a specific electrical circuit: a small lamp designed to work with a 1.5-volt battery, with wires connecting the lamp to both battery terminals.

There is a complete conducting connection through the wires and lamp, together with the processes inside the battery. This is a **closed circuit**.

When the circuit is closed, charge can move continuously. The battery transfers chemical energy into electrical energy, and the lamp transfers electrical energy into light and heat.

If one connection is broken, the circuit is **open**. There is no steady current around that circuit, and the lamp goes out.

But the battery can still have a voltage between its terminals.

**Voltage can exist even when there is no steady current.**

An unconnected battery is a familiar example. Its terminals have a voltage difference while it sits unused.

To understand how charges begin moving, we need the term **electric field**.

An electric field describes the electrical force that a charge would experience at a particular place.

Charges produce electric fields. When charges rearrange in a circuit, they change the electric field in and around the circuit.

In a metal wire, that field acts on the electrons. It causes their motion to have an overall direction.

The electrons are already moving microscopically within the metal. When current flows, they also have a small average movement along the wire. This average movement is called **drift**.

The electrical change that starts current can spread through a circuit very quickly. The electrons’ average movement along the wire can be much slower.

That is why a lamp can turn on quickly even though an individual electron moves slowly along the wire. Electrons are already present throughout the circuit.

Electric fields and voltage describe related things:

- An **electric field** tells us about the force on a charge at a place.
- A **voltage difference** tells us about the change in electrical energy per amount of charge between places.

Now we can describe **current** more carefully.

**Current tells us how much charge passes a chosen place in a circuit each second.**

We measure current in **amperes**, usually shortened to **amps**. The letter **A** stands for amperes.

**One amp means one coulomb per second.**

Written with units:

**1 A = 1 C/s**

So a current of 2 amps means that two coulombs of charge pass the chosen place every second.

Voltage and current answer different questions:

- **Voltage:** How much energy can be transferred for each coulomb?
- **Current:** How many coulombs pass each second?

A circuit could have a large voltage and a tiny current. Another circuit could have a smaller voltage and a much larger current.

The current depends on the whole circuit, including its **resistance**.

Resistance describes how much a component limits current for a given voltage.

We measure resistance in **ohms**. The symbol for ohms is **Ω**, a Greek letter called omega.

A component made to have a particular resistance is called a **resistor**.

For a resistor with a steady resistance:

- Increasing the voltage across it increases the current.
- Increasing its resistance, while keeping the voltage the same, decreases the current.

The relationship is called **Ohm’s law**:

**Voltage = current × resistance**

Using letters:

**V = I × R**

Here:

- **V** means voltage, measured in volts.
- **I** means current, measured in amps.
- **R** means resistance, measured in ohms.

The letter for current is **I**. That is simply the letter commonly used for it.

We can also write Ohm’s law this way:

**Current = voltage ÷ resistance**

For example, suppose a resistor has a resistance of **3 ohms**, and there are **6 volts** across it.

Then:

**6 ÷ 3 = 2 amps**

The current is 2 amps.

Keep that same 3-ohm resistance, but increase the voltage to 12 volts:

**12 ÷ 3 = 4 amps**

Twice the voltage gives twice the current, because the resistance stayed the same.

Now keep the voltage at 6 volts, but use a resistance of 6 ohms:

**6 ÷ 6 = 1 amp**

Twice the resistance gives half the current, because the voltage stayed the same.

Ohm’s law is especially useful for components whose resistance stays nearly constant.

Some electrical components behave differently. For example, a lamp’s thin metal filament changes resistance as it gets hot. A small electronic light called an LED also needs a different description of how its current changes with voltage.

So the simple calculations above apply when treating the resistance as constant is a good description.

What happens inside a resistor?

Moving electrons interact with the material. Electrical energy is transferred to the material, making it warmer.

The electrons continue through the circuit. The resistor receives energy while the amount of charge is conserved.

The same idea applies to a lamp: charge moves through it, and energy is transferred to it.

A useful question is how quickly a device receives energy. That quantity is called **power**.

We measure power in **watts**, written **W**.

**One watt means one joule of energy transferred each second.**

For a simple circuit with steady voltage and current:

**Power = voltage × current**

Suppose a component has 6 volts across it and a current of 2 amps through it.

Then:

**6 × 2 = 12 watts**

Here is what that means:

The voltage says that **each coulomb transfers 6 joules**.

The current says that **2 coulombs pass each second**.

Together, they mean that **12 joules are transferred each second**.

That is 12 watts.

This also helps explain why a battery’s voltage does not tell you all its properties.

Two batteries can both be 1.5 volts but store different amounts of energy.

When each supplies 1.5 volts, it transfers about 1.5 joules for each coulomb passing through the whole circuit. But one battery may be able to keep doing that for much longer.

To know how long a battery can operate a device, you also need information about its stored energy, the current the device uses, and how the battery behaves while supplying it.

The voltage across an individual component also depends on how the circuit is connected.

Suppose two identical resistors are connected **one after the other** to a 6-volt battery. The same current passes through both.

Each resistor has 3 volts across it. Together, their voltage differences add up to the battery’s 6 volts.

For each coulomb passing through the circuit, the battery supplies 6 joules. Each resistor receives 3 joules.

Now suppose each resistor is connected directly between the battery’s two terminals, giving charge two separate conducting routes. Each resistor then has the full 6 volts across it.

So the words **“across a component”** matter. They mean we are comparing the voltage at that component’s two connections.

A **voltmeter** measures this difference.

It has two measuring leads. Each lead makes contact with one of the two places being compared.

If the meter reads 1.5 volts across a battery, it has measured a difference between those two terminals.

If the measuring leads are reversed, the meter may read −1.5 volts.

The minus sign tells us that the order of the comparison has reversed. The size of the difference is still 1.5 volts.

Voltage can also change over time.

A battery normally maintains the same positive and negative terminals. In a simple battery circuit, current keeps the same overall direction. This is called **direct current**, or **DC**.

An electrical supply can instead repeatedly reverse its voltage. This can make current repeatedly reverse direction. That is **alternating current**, or **AC**.

A suitable lamp or heater can receive energy while current moves in either direction.

Batteries are only one source of electrical energy. Solar cells transfer energy from light. Generators transfer energy from motion. Each uses physical processes that can produce a voltage and supply current.

Charges can also collect on an object’s surface. This can create a voltage difference between that object and its surroundings. A spark is a brief current through air when conditions allow the air to conduct.

Throughout all these examples, the meaning of voltage stays the same.

**A 6-volt difference corresponds to 6 joules of electrical energy for every coulomb of charge transferred through that difference.** The current tells you how much charge moves each second, and together they tell you how quickly energy is transferred.

answer:
Voltage is a measure of how much electrical energy is available to move electric charge from one place to another. Its scientific name is **electric potential difference**. Voltage is measured in **volts**, whose symbol is **V**.

To understand voltage, we need to start with matter and electric charge.

## Atoms and electric charge

Everything you can touch is made of tiny building blocks called **atoms**. An atom has even smaller parts:

- **Protons** have positive electric charge.
- **Electrons** have negative electric charge.
- **Neutrons** have no electric charge.

Protons and neutrons are packed together in an atom’s center, called its **nucleus**. Electrons are found around the nucleus. In many materials, some electrons can move from one atom to another.

An object is usually electrically neutral when it has equal amounts of positive and negative charge. If it gains extra electrons, it has more negative charge than positive charge. If it loses electrons, it has more positive charge than negative charge.

Electric charge is measured in **coulombs**. The symbol for charge is usually **Q**.

## What voltage measures

Voltage tells us how much energy is available for each unit of electric charge. More precisely:

**Voltage = energy transferred ÷ charge**

In symbols:

**V = E ÷ Q**

Here, **V** is voltage, **E** is energy, and **Q** is charge.

One volt means one joule of energy for each coulomb of charge:

**1 V = 1 J ÷ 1 C**

So a 9-volt battery can provide up to 9 joules of energy for each coulomb of charge that passes through it, under the conditions in which it is being used.

Voltage is always measured **between two points**. Saying “this point is 5 volts” is incomplete unless we say what other point it is 5 volts compared with. In a circuit, one point is often chosen as the reference and called **ground**. Ground is not necessarily connected to the Earth; it is simply the circuit’s chosen zero-voltage reference.

## What a battery does

A battery uses chemical reactions to separate electric charges. Those reactions make one terminal have a higher electric potential than the other terminal.

For example, a 1.5-volt battery has a potential difference of about 1.5 volts between its terminals. When a complete circuit connects the terminals, the battery can transfer energy to charges moving through that circuit.

The battery does not create electrons from nothing. Charges are already present in the wires and parts of the circuit. The battery supplies energy that helps drive those charges around the complete path.

## Voltage and current are different

**Current** is the rate at which electric charge flows. It is measured in **amperes**, or amps. One amp means one coulomb of charge passing a point each second.

Voltage describes energy per charge. Current describes charge flow per second. They are related, but they are not the same thing.

A circuit can have voltage across two points even when no current is flowing. For example, a battery that is not connected to anything still has voltage between its terminals. Current flows only when there is a complete path and the circuit’s conditions allow charge to move.

## How voltage moves charges

When there is a voltage difference across a conducting material, it creates an electric field in that material. The field exerts forces on charged particles. In a metal wire, electrons drift through the wire in response to this field.

The electrons’ average drift is usually slow, even though the electrical effects of changing a circuit can spread through it very quickly. Also, the electrons do not generally travel all the way from the battery, through a lamp, and back in one quick trip. Electrons already throughout the wire begin moving when the circuit’s electric field is established.

In metal wires, electrons move from the battery’s negative terminal toward its positive terminal. By convention, however, **electric current** is described as flowing from the positive side toward the negative side through the external circuit. This convention was established before scientists understood that electrons carry charge in metals.

## Voltage across a part of a circuit

When current passes through a lamp, motor, or other circuit part, that part can receive electrical energy. The voltage across it describes how much energy is transferred per unit of charge as charge moves through it.

For example, if 2 coulombs of charge transfer 10 joules of energy through a component, the voltage across the component is:

**V = 10 J ÷ 2 C = 5 V**

The energy may become light, heat, sound, motion, or some combination, depending on the component.

## Ohm’s law

For many common materials and components, voltage, current, and resistance are related by **Ohm’s law**:

**V = I × R**

- **V** is voltage, measured in volts.
- **I** is current, measured in amps.
- **R** is resistance, measured in ohms.

Resistance describes how strongly a component opposes electric current. A larger resistance means less current for the same voltage. For example, if a 6-volt voltage is across a 3-ohm resistor:

**I = V ÷ R = 6 V ÷ 3 Ω = 2 A**

Ohm’s law works well for many resistors, but not for every electrical device in every situation. A light bulb’s filament, a diode, and a battery can behave in ways that do not follow the simple rule across all conditions.

## Voltage does not tell you everything

A higher voltage does not automatically mean that more current is flowing. The current also depends on the circuit’s resistance and other properties. A high-voltage source with a very high resistance may allow little current. A lower-voltage source connected to a very low resistance may allow a large current.

Voltage alone also does not tell you how much total energy a battery can supply. That depends on how much charge the battery can move and how its chemistry behaves. A small battery and a large battery can have the same voltage but store different amounts of energy.

## A careful summary

- Atoms contain protons, neutrons, and electrons.
- Electric charge is a property of particles; electrons are negatively charged.
- Voltage is the difference in electric potential between two points.
- It measures energy available or transferred per unit of charge.
- Current measures how quickly charge flows.
- Resistance affects how much current flows for a given voltage.
- In many circuits, voltage, current, and resistance are related by **V = I × R**.
- A voltage difference can exist without current, but current in a circuit requires a complete path.

answer:
# What Is Voltage?

Voltage is a way to describe how much **energy each bit of electric charge can gain or lose when it moves between two places**.

The scientific definition is:

**Voltage = energy transferred ÷ electric charge**

The unit of voltage is the **volt**, written **V**. One volt means that one coulomb of charge transfers one joule of energy:

**1 volt = 1 joule per coulomb**

A coulomb is a quantity of electric charge, and a joule is a quantity of energy.

## First: What Is Electricity?

Electricity involves **electric charge** and what charged particles do.

There are two kinds of electric charge:

- **Positive charge**
- **Negative charge**

The centers of atoms contain positively charged particles called **protons**. Atoms also contain **neutrons**, which have no electric charge. Negatively charged **electrons** are found in states around the atom’s center.

An atom usually has the same number of protons and electrons, so its total charge is zero. But electrons can sometimes move from one place to another. If an object gains extra electrons, it becomes negatively charged. If it loses electrons, it becomes positively charged.

Charges affect other charges: positive and negative charges attract each other, and charges of the same kind repel each other. These effects are part of electricity.

## How Voltage Relates to Charge

When charge moves, energy can be transferred. Voltage tells us how much energy is transferred **for each unit of charge** between two points.

For example, if one coulomb of charge transfers two joules of energy while moving between two points, the voltage difference between those points is two volts.

Voltage is always measured **between two points**. Saying “this point is at 5 volts” only makes sense if we know what other point it is being compared with. In a circuit, that comparison point is often called **ground** or **zero volts**.

## What Happens in a Circuit?

A circuit is a path through which electric charge can move. In a metal wire, some electrons can move through the material. When a source, such as a battery, creates a voltage between two parts of a connected circuit, an electric field forms in the circuit. That field affects charges throughout the circuit.

If the path is complete, charge moves through it. The moving charge is called **electric current**. As charge passes through a device, such as a lamp, the device can receive energy from the moving charges and change that energy into light, heat, motion, or another form.

The voltage describes the energy transferred per amount of charge. The current describes how much charge passes a point each second. They describe different things.

- **Voltage:** energy transferred per charge
- **Current:** charge moving per second

A circuit can have voltage even when charge is not flowing. For example, a battery that is not connected to anything still has a voltage between its terminals. With no complete path, there is no steady current through an outside circuit.

## What Does a Battery Do?

Inside a battery, chemical processes move charge in ways that keep one terminal at a different electric potential from the other. This creates a voltage between the terminals.

When the battery is connected to a complete circuit, the battery’s chemical processes provide energy to the charges. The charges can then transfer energy to devices in the circuit.

A battery marked **1.5 V** transfers about **1.5 joules of energy per coulomb of charge** through the circuit, under the conditions where that voltage applies.

## What Are Ohms and Ohm’s Law?

**Resistance** describes how much a component limits current for a given voltage. Resistance is measured in **ohms**, written with the symbol **Ω**.

For many common circuit components, voltage, current, and resistance are related by **Ohm’s law**:

**V = I × R**

Here:

- **V** is voltage in volts
- **I** is current in amperes
- **R** is resistance in ohms

Suppose a component has a resistance of 2 ohms and a current of 3 amperes through it. The voltage across it is:

**V = 3 × 2 = 6 volts**

Ohm’s law describes many useful components, but not every electrical component behaves according to it in all situations.

## Which Way Do Electrons Move?

In a metal wire, the moving charges are usually electrons. Electrons have negative charge, so their overall movement is opposite to the direction called **conventional current**.

Conventional current is defined as the direction positive charge would move. Scientists and engineers often use this direction when drawing and discussing circuits, even in wires where electrons are the charges that move.

## How Is Voltage Measured?

A **voltmeter** measures the voltage difference between two points. To measure the voltage across a component, the meter is connected to both ends of that component.

Voltage is not a material that flows through wires. It describes an energy difference per charge between places. Current, by contrast, describes charge moving through a circuit.

## The Main Idea

Voltage tells you how much energy can be transferred for each amount of electric charge as charge moves between two points. A battery can create voltage; a complete circuit lets current flow; and components can receive energy from that current.

answer:
McCulloch’s hostility to psychoanalysis is best understood as a struggle over **what counts as an explanation of the mind**. But “pathologically opposed” risks assuming the very diagnosis that needs explaining. His opposition had intellectual and institutional reasons; an account of his personal motives would require evidence beyond the intensity of his polemics.

One preliminary correction matters: Warren McCulloch was a founding figure in neural-network research, alongside Walter Pitts. Their 1943 paper, “A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity,” showed how networks of idealized neurons could implement logical operations. Calling him *the* inventor obscures both Pitts’s contribution and the distance between their formal neurons and today’s neural networks.

**Why oppose psychoanalysis?**

McCulloch trained in medicine and psychiatry, but his preferred explanations joined neurophysiology, experimental science, and mathematical logic. Psychoanalytic explanations invoked unconscious wishes, repression, and interpretations whose evidentiary status he distrusted. The disagreement concerned not simply whether unconscious processes exist—his own framework readily accommodated processes inaccessible to awareness—but how one could establish what those processes were.

For McCulloch, an explanation should specify a mechanism capable of producing the phenomenon. An analyst’s reconstruction of a symptom’s meaning did not necessarily meet that requirement. Psychoanalysis also represented a rival professional authority within psychiatry: the dispute concerned who could legitimately speak about mental life and what methods entitled them to do so.

Nevertheless, it would be misleading to turn McCulloch into a straightforward behaviorist who denied interior life. His central question was precisely how material nervous systems could support perception, knowledge, and purposes. He wanted to explain mind through mechanisms, and those mechanisms could be recursive, embodied, and remarkably complex.

**What might this have done to AI?**

The strongest claim is about an intellectual orientation, not a single causal chain. McCulloch helped make it plausible to approach intelligence through formally describable operations. In that orientation, a machine need not possess an interpretable personal history to count as performing an intelligent act.

This helped open a productive research program: build mechanisms, demonstrate capacities, and compare their behavior with that of organisms. It also made certain questions easier to put aside:

- Whether a system’s apparently rational activity expresses conflicting motivations.
- Whether speech conceals, displaces, or transforms what a subject wants.
- Whether intelligence can be understood apart from attachment, dependency, sexuality, and personal history.
- Whether a system’s failures reveal something constitutive about its organization rather than merely a defect.

Those are questions psychoanalysis keeps in view, although it does not have exclusive ownership of them.

There are limits to this historical argument. **AI’s relative neglect of psychoanalysis cannot be attributed to McCulloch’s hostility alone.** Military funding, engineering methods, available computers, behaviorism, and later cognitive psychology all mattered. Moreover, McCulloch’s neural-network program differed substantially from the symbolic AI that became prominent after the 1950s. “Anti-Freudianism produced AI” is much too simple.

There is also an irony: psychoanalysis and cybernetics were not sealed worlds. Jacques Lacan engaged with cybernetics, and Gregory Bateson brought communication theory into psychiatric inquiry. Formal accounts of information and psychoanalytic accounts of subjectivity could interact, even where McCulloch would have resisted the result.

**In what sense did he “instrumentalize” mental illness?**

This needs a distinction between using psychiatric patients as experimental subjects, using diagnostic categories as explanatory models, and using pathology as a way to investigate normal functioning. These are different historical claims and require different evidence.

The defensible general point is that McCulloch’s program made psychiatric disturbance available as a problem of **functional organization**. Instead of asking only what a symptom meant within a biography, one could ask what organization of excitation, inhibition, memory, and feedback could generate it. Pathology could thereby become an investigative instrument: disturbances might expose the organization that ordinary functioning conceals.

But we should not invent a tidy McCullochian dictionary in which neurosis means one circuit defect, psychosis another, and schizophrenia a third. His 1943 neural-network paper does not supply such a clinical theory. Nor should Bateson and his collaborators’ later “double bind” hypothesis of schizophrenia be credited to McCulloch. They belonged to overlapping cybernetic conversations, but their claims were distinct.

The deeper transformation is this: **a symptom can become evidence about a system’s architecture rather than an expression to be interpreted.** That can yield experimentally useful questions. It can also strip suffering of biography and social context if the functional account is treated as exhaustive.

Even here, however, McCulloch complicates the picture. His 1945 paper on a “heterarchy of values” explored how nervous organization could produce preferences that do not fit a single consistent ranking. His work did not simply equate intelligence with an internally unified, perfectly consistent rational agent.

**Was Philip K. Dick onto something with the schizoid android?**

Yes—as a philosophical and literary provocation, rather than a clinical prediction.

“Schizoid,” “schizophrenic,” and “psychotic” are not interchangeable. Schizoid generally concerns detachment and restricted interpersonal engagement; schizophrenia is a different diagnostic category. Neither diagnosis entails an absence of empathy or humanity. Dick’s androids should therefore not be read as accurate representations of psychiatric patients.

What Dick exposes, especially in *Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?*, is the instability of identifying humanity with a measurable capacity. The android may display intelligence, language, planning, and self-preservation while its claim to moral consideration is denied through an empathy test. Meanwhile, supposedly human society itself displays cruelty, instrumental treatment of others, and compromised forms of fellow feeling.

That gives your connection real force: **if intelligence is operationalized as successful performance, what happens to everything that successful performance fails to establish about a being?** Does it suffer? Does it care? Does its history matter? Do we owe it anything?

Dick also turns the question back on the examiner. The authority that diagnoses an entity as deficient may itself be participating in a profoundly dehumanizing institution.

The strongest connection, then, is not that McCulloch accidentally built schizophrenia into AI. It is that a science capable of explaining intelligent operations can still leave unresolved the status of the being performing them. Dick makes that unresolved remainder the center of the story.
